title: 3-Read Friday #121
author: Craig Barton
summary: In this week's 3-Read Friday, Craig Barton curates three pieces of education writing around a single tension: what teachers and researchers can and cannot infer from small, proxy measures of learning. The first item, Benjamin Riley's response to a large-scale Chinese study, argues that generative AI use produced homework-score gains that masked a real decline in exam performance for a huge share of students who effectively outsourced their thinking. The second, Dominic Salles's piece, questions the classroom orthodoxy of rapid attention-checks, arguing that treating attention as the goal rather than a proxy for learning can crowd out the deeper processing teachers actually want. The third, Becky Allen's reflection on a podcast about teaching the volume of a prism, uses two equally well-trained Direct Instruction designers producing different sequences to ask where instructional judgment actually resides if not in stated theory alone. Barton's own framing ties the three together: each is a case study in mistaking an easy-to-measure signal (homework score, attention, theoretical fidelity) for the harder-to-see reality (genuine learning, understanding, expert judgment) underneath it.
points: Barton's selection turns on a single idea running through all three picks: proxies for learning (homework scores, visible attention, adherence to instructional theory) can diverge sharply from the learning itself, and each linked author catches a different version of that gap.

By pairing Riley's AI-and-homework study with Salles's attention-checking critique, the roundup implicitly argues that two of education's most trusted immediate feedback signals — a completed assignment and a visibly attentive class — are exactly the signals most vulnerable to being gamed or misread.

Barton's choice to feature Becky Allen's prism episode, about his own podcast, signals that even a well-specified pedagogical theory (Direct Instruction, atomisation) leaves real design decisions to a form of tacit expertise that theory alone doesn't settle.
quotes: A new study has come out on the effects of AI on learning… and it's not great news for an AI optimist like me.
Drawing on 27,000 Chinese students, the study suggests that half have outsourced the thinking altogether, with consequences that positive homework scores obscure.
Dominic argues that they can actively get in the way of learning, because attention is only ever a proxy, and optimising the proxy costs you the thing itself.
Becky argues that the episode exposes a gap that Kris Boulton's work on atomisation cannot fill.
If two designers steeped in the same Direct Instruction principles produce two very different sequences, where does the knowledge that picks the better one actually live?
